title: Part V: Advanced Prepayment & Greeks
text:
Having constructed two forward curves for short rates, we now return to the topic of prepayment. At a high level, borrower prepayments are influenced by two primary drivers:

Refinance Incentive (Refi): Borrowers refinance when market interest rates drop, allowing them to secure a new loan with a lower rate. This type of prepayment is highly sensitive to changes in market rates. When the spread between the borrower’s original loan rate and current market rates increases, refinancing becomes more attractive, leading to a rise in prepayments.
Demographics (Demo): Life events, such as job relocation, retirement, family changes, or downsizing, also drive prepayments. These demographic-driven prepayments are less influenced by interest rates and are tied more closely to the borrower’s circumstances and the age of the loan.



The mortgage rate from the market is known as the Primary Current Coupoon (PCC). In order to project it into the future, we are going to use a very simple model:
\[
PCC(t) = \text{DiscountRate}(t) + \text{PccSpread}
\]
Where \(\text{DiscountRate}(t)\) represents the short rate, and PccSpread is a fixed spread that accounts for additional costs or market factors. While this PCC model isn’t very realistic, it allows us to better represent prepayment behavior in our analysis. Use 3.3% as your spread.



The refinance component of our prepay model is defined as:
\[
refi(spread(t)) =
\begin{cases}
\begin{aligned}
&0 & \text{if } spread < 0, \\
&\ slope \cdot spread & \text{if } 0 \leq spread \leq .015, \\
&.0425 & \text{if } spread > .015
\end{aligned}
\end{cases}
\]
 Where:

\(slope = \frac{.0425}{.015}\)
\(spread(t) = GrossCoupon - PCC(t)\)

 
Refi maps the refinancing spread to prepayment behavior, with stronger incentives leading to higher prepayment rates.



Our modeled demographic prepayments depend on two factors: the age of the mortgage and seasonal trends:
\[
demo(t) = seasoning(age(t)) \cdot seasonal(month\_of\_year(t))
\]

Seasoning: Prepayments are low when a loan is new, gradually increasing to a stable long-term rate. The seasoning factor ramps linearly from 0 to a base SMM over the first 18 months of the loan’s life. For these exercises use .5% for your base SMM.
Seasonality: Prepayment rates exhibit predictable seasonal trends, with spikes in the summer and dips in the winter. The seasonal factor scales prepayment rates accordingly based on the month. See the code block below for the month to scalars map.




Our new prepayment model combines these components to better capture borrower behavior and prepayment optionality:
\[
SMM(t) = refi(spread(t)) + demo(t)
\]
Here:

\(spread(t)\): GrossCoupon - PCC(t)
\(t\): Time in months from the first of the market close’s month. E.g. If the market close is 1/15/2024 then \(t\) is the time to 1/1/2024

These models provide a more nuanced representation of prepayment dynamics, improving the realism of our simulations.

NB: There are a lot of moving parts here. Remember that changing your OAS should not change your cash flows. I would make sure this is the case. Shocking your discount rates will definitely change your cash flows because your PCC is a funciton of those rates.

In the fixed-income world, this phenomenon is referred to as Negative Convexity. It arises because the owner of an MBS or mortgage is effectively long a fixed-income amortizing bond while being short an American option that allows for prepayment.

title: Part V: Advanced Prepayment & Greeks
text:
Problem 19: Derivatives
The Taylor’s Series gives us a quick way to compute a second order approximation to the change in MBS value given a change in rates.
The first derivative with respect to rates is known as the Dollar Value of an 01 (DV01). The ‘01’ can be one percent or one basis point. These exercises will use one percent. This is closely related to Duration, but I want to stick with the raw derivative for simplicity.
\[DV01 = \frac{V(up) - V(dn)}{2 \cdot shock}\]
where:

shock is the amount to bump the discount rates
V(up) is the value given a positive bump amount
V(dn) is the value given a negative bump amount

The second derivative is known as convexity or gamma and is defined by:
\[Convexity = \frac{V(up) + V(dn) - 2 \cdot V(md)}{shock^2}\]
Where:

V(md) is the base value, i.e. where shock is zero.

Example output:

text:
Problem 20: Multi-Path Valuation
If you run our favorite MBS along the rates given above, the rates from your bootstrapped curve, and the rates from your smoother curve you will see each produces a different value. What’s worse is that individually they do a poor job of capturing the value of the optionality embedded in the security. We would like to run a large number of possible trajectories through time and compute the value as the average of the trajectory values.
Write a function that takes a vector of dates, a matrix of discount rate trajectories, and values our standard MBS with an OAS of 3%. This is mostly an exercise in plumbing, so your paths are the rates given above, a 50 basis point shock up, and a 50 basis point shock down. Even though there are only three trajectories in this problem, write your code to be general enough to take an arbitrary number of paths.

title: Part VI: Monte Carlo
text:
In order to generate Monte Carlo paths of rates, we will use the classic Hull-White model for short rates. I don’t care if you find the code online or write it up yourself. If you choose to roll your own, here are some helpful notes.

The one-factor Hull-White model describes the evolution of short-term interest rates \(r(t)\) using the stochastic differential equation (SDE):
\[dr(t) = [\theta(t) - \alpha r(t)] dt + \sigma \, dW(t)\]



Mean Reversion:

The term $ -r(t)$ pulls the rate $ r(t) $ toward a time-dependent mean.
$ > 0 $ is the mean reversion speed.

Volatility:

\(\sigma\) represents the volatility of the short rate, scaled by the Brownian motion $ W(t) $.

Time-Dependent Drift \(\theta(t)\):

Ensures the model fits the initial term structure of interest rates (e.g., yield curves).


To simulate this model using Monte Carlo, the SDE is discretized using the Euler-Maruyama scheme:
\[
r_{t+\Delta t} = r_t + \left(\theta(t) - \alpha r_t\right)\Delta t + \sigma \sqrt{\Delta t} \, Z_t
\]
where:

\(r_t\): Short rate from your forward curve at time \(t\).
\(\Delta t\): Time step size.
\(Z_t\): Random variable sampled from a standard normal distribution (\(Z_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\)).

To compute \(\theta(t_i)\) for Monte Carlo simulation:
\[
\theta(t_i) = \frac{f_{t_{i+1}} - f_{t_i}}{\Delta t} + \alpha f_{t_i} + \frac{\sigma^2}{2\alpha} \left(1 - e^{-2\alpha t_i}\right)
\]
Where \(f_t\) is the continuously compounounded forward rate from your forward curve. I usually choose my grid so that the \(t\) always hits a knot point on my step discount rate function so no interpolation is required.





Initialize:

Set the starting short rate \(r_0\) with the initial rate of your forward curve.

Iterate Over Time Steps:

For each time step, compute \(r_{t+\Delta t}\) using the discretized equation.

Simulate Paths:

Repeat the process across multiple paths by drawing independent random samples \(Z_t\) for each path.

Aggregate Results:

Use the simulated short-rate paths to compute expectations, price derivatives, or analyze the distribution of rates.


NB: Smaller \(\Delta t\) improves accuracy but increases computational cost. We will explore variance reduction techniques in another problem.

Let’s return to the topic of discount factors. Each trajectory/path of your monte carlo simulation produces a rate function that you can use to discount future cash flows. Our discount factors are now stochastic (SDF). It is important to keep in mind that the SDFs are not zero coupon bonds. However, the average of all those pathwise SDFs are equal to the correspsonding ZCB:
\[ZCB(t, T) = \mathbb{E}[SDF(t, T)] = \mathbb{E}[e^{-\int_t^T{r(u)du}}]\]

Example Output:
In order to check the correctness of your implementation, we need to look at the following things:

The variance of your simulated short rate \(r_t\) is approximately: \[\frac{\sigma^2}{2 \alpha} (1-e^{-2 \alpha t})\]
The average SDF(\(t\)) over your monte carlo paths is approximately the ZCB(\(t\)) from your forward curve
The variance of SDF(\(t\)) is approximately:

\[
\left(\frac{\sigma}{\alpha}\right)^2 \left( t
+ \frac{2}{\alpha} e^{-\alpha t}
- \frac{1}{2\alpha} e^{-2\alpha t}
- \frac{3}{2\alpha} \right)
\]

If you look at the results above, you may notice that the variances can be quite high and the Monte Carlo values are a bit off from what we get from our forward curve. .5, -.25, .01, .02, ...

-.5 .25, -.01, -.02, ...

title: Part II: Prepayment & Dates
text:
Recall that we allow the borrower to prepay their loan. There are a number of reasons why this may happen:

The borrower gets a job in a new city
The borrower finds a lower rate in the current market
The borrower outgrows (or downsizes from) their current home due to changes in the size of their family
If the loan balance is significantly lower than the value of the home, the borrower can take out a new loan with a higher balance, pay off the old loan, and keep the difference. This is known as a Cash Out.

We referred to the projected balances as “scheduled” in previous exercises because they don’t include prepayments. Now we are going to add prepayments to our code. The Single Monthly Mortality (SMM) rate is the percentage of the pool that prepays in a particular month. We use it to compute the fraction of the original pool that remains:
\(pool(0) = 1\)
\(pool(t) = pool(t-1) * [1 - SMM(t-1)]\)
We use this to project the \(\textit{actual balance}\) (\(B\))
\(B(t) = ScheduledBalance(t) * pool(t)\)

Your output can contain other helpful fields, such as the SMM, too.
NB: One can’t technically prepay in the period from \(M-1\) to \(M\) because all pools pay off at maturity under our assumptions.

title: Part II: Prepayment & Dates
text:
Problem 8: Weighted Average Life
The common perception of a bond is one of a bullet, where the balance remains constant until maturity, at which time the entire principal is paid off. A mortgage bond, however, amortizes throughout its life, meaning the balance changes before maturity. In the case of an amortizing bond, it is useful to know its Weighted Average Life (WAL) to get a sense of the average time it takes for the lender or investor to receive all their principal back. You can read the basics here:
Weighted-average life (Wikipedia)
Write a function that takes a vector of balances, a vector of accrual dates, a vector of payment dates, and a reference date, and computes the WAL. The function could also just take a reference date and a dataframe that contains balance, accrual date, and payment date.

A few words about the reference date:
The reference date is actually the trade settle date, which is the day the investor pays for and takes ownership of the bond. There is a wrinkle about which future cash flows the investor owns. The investor is entitled to all cash flows based on the balance of the bond at the time of purchase. One source of confusion is if the purchase happens before the payment date. For instance, let’s assume one buys a bond on the 5th of the month that has a payment delay of 24 days, implying the next cash flow will fall on the 25th of the month. The investor is not entitled to this cash flow because it is based on the previous month’s balance.
Assume the number of days in a year is a constant 365 when computing the number of years between payment dates and the settle date.

title: Part I: Mortgage Basics
text:
Problem 1: Mortgage Payment
The length of a loan is known as its term. Common terms include 15 and 30 years. We sometimes refer to an original term to differentiate it from the remaining term, which is the remaining life of an aged loan. For clarity:
\[
\text{term} = \text{original term} = \text{age} + \text{remaining term}
\]
A borrower must pay an interest rate for a mortgage, known as its coupon. For reasons that will be clear later, we will refer to the borrower’s coupon as the gross coupon. This coupon is quoted as an annual rate, but we will always divide it by 12 (the number of months in a year) when computing owed interest. In our case, the interest owed will be the loan balance at the beginning of the period times the coupon divided by 12.
Given a term \(M\) in months, a gross coupon \(C\), and an initial loan amount \(B\), derive a formula for the constant monthly payment \(P\) such that:
\(B(0) = B\)
\(B(1) = B(0) * (1 + C/12) - P\)
…
\(B(t) = B(t-1) * (1 + C/12) - P\)
…
\(B(M)\) = 0
NB: If you haven’t reviewed geometric series recently, you might want to revisit the topic.

Problem 4: Mortgage Backed Securities
When creating a Mortgage Backed Security (MBS), a financial institution will combine many “similar” loans into a single pool and sell them to an investor. In many cases, the financial institution creates a Pass-Through bond, which means they continue to collect the borrower’s payments, take a small Servicing Fee (typically 0.25% of the pool balance), and pass the remaining amount to the investor. The investor is entitled to all the principal paid, but the servicing fee comes out of the interest paid. The Net Coupon is the gross coupon less the servicing and other fees. We only care about the former and assume the latter is zero.
NB: The scheduled balances are computed with the gross coupon, but the interest paid to the investor is computed with the net coupon.
It is convenient to think of a pool of loans as a single loan, where attributes such as the gross coupon are the balance-weighted gross coupon of the individual loans in the pool, and attributes such as balance are the sum of the individual balances.

title: Part III: Discounting & Pricing
text:
Problem 10: Present Value
Now that we have a way to compute \(ZCBs\) we can use them to compute the time \(t\) value, \(V(t)\), by taking the dot product of the vector of future cash flows with a vector of \(ZCBs\) that correspond to the payment (as opposed to the accrual) dates relative to the time \(t\).
The basic steps are:

Use the settle and accrual dates to determine the cash flows the investor bought
Use the settle date to determine time t for discounting
For each relevant payment date \(T_n\), compute the \(ZCB(t, T_n)\)
Take the dot product of your cash flow and \(ZCB\) vectors to compute \(V(t)\)

In the case where \(t>0\) the quantity computed is called a forward value. This is the number of dollars one would buy or sell the instrument at time \(t\).

title: Part III: Discounting & Pricing
text:
Problem 11: Price
In the previous problem, we computed the present value of all future cash flows relative to the trade settle date. Now, we want to focus on how the bond price would be quoted in the market. Ultimately, we aim to calculate the clean price.
To start, we normalize the value by multiplying it by 100 and dividing it by the balance at the settle date. This gives us the dirty price. In other words:
\[
\text{Dirty Price} = \text{Value} \times \frac{100}{\text{Balance at Settle}}
\]
For a detailed explanation of the terms dirty price and clean price, refer to the following resources:

Dirty Price (Wikipedia)
Clean Price (Wikipedia)

Both articles mention the concept of accrued interest. Before we compute accrued interest for our bond, we need to understand day count conventions. You can read more about them here:

Day Count Convention (Wikipedia)

Our bond uses the 30/360 day count method. We need to compute the interest accrued from the partial period that runs from the first of the trade settle month to the trade settle date. Excel has a function called DAYS360 that is useful for computing this quantity.
Task: Write a function that computes the simplest 30/360 method described on Wikipedia (Bond Basis) and use it in another function to convert a (dirty) value to a clean price. It is acceptable to report the dirty price and accrued interest as well.

title: Part III: Discounting & Pricing
text:
Problem 12: Option Adjusted Spread
The prices generated using the logic above often (if not always) differ from the market-observed prices of MBS. To reconcile this difference, an Option Adjusted Spread (OAS) is added to the discount rates.
To keep things easier let’s work with values instead of prices. Given a discount date grid, discount rate grid, settlement date, cash flows, and a target value, write a function to compute the OAS that aligns the computed price with the target value.
NB: This is only involves discounting. It doesn’t change your cash flows. The OAS is a constant spread applied to the continuously compounded discount rates. Since the spreads may vary across securities, it’s advisable not to adjust the discount rates directly.
NB: I am ignoring a technical issue for forward settles here. My forward value equation is:
\[ V(t, OAS) = \frac{V(0, OAS)}{ZCB(t, OAS)}\]
instead of
\[ V(t, OAS) = \frac{V(0, OAS)}{ZCB(t, 0.0)}\]

title: Part IV: Forward Curves
text:
To calibrate a forward curve using market inputs, we first need to generate cash flows for our calibration instruments. Although mortgage shops typically use a SOFR-based curve, calculating the floating rate side of a SOFR swap is tedious and doesn’t add much to the inutituion of curve construction. Therefore, we’ll use Constant Maturity Treasuries (\(\textit{CMTs}\)) instead. CMTs are hypothetical bullet bonds that behave like Treasury bonds if they were issued daily, with spot par coupons published by the U.S. Treasury Department.
Task: Create a function that generates the cash flows for these bonds. The function should take the following inputs:

Bond Effective date (start date of the bond)
Balance (face amount)
Annual coupon rate (in decimal form)
Number of years (as an integer)

The function should return two vectors:

The payment dates
The corresponding bond cash flows

The first cash flow should occur six months from the effective date, and the final one should be paid the specified number of years after the effective date. Each cash flow should include the coupon payment (calculated as balance * coupon / 2), with the final cash flow also including the principal repayment. title: Part IV: Forward Curves
text:
Problem 14: Forward Curve - Bootstrapping
A forward curve of instantaneous discount rates is a function that maps future points in time to discount rates. This function helps determine the present value of cash flows occurring at those specific future dates. The formulas are the same as the ninth problem above that deals with ZCBs.
Forward curves aren’t directly observable and must be calibrated from market prices or yields of financial instruments like bonds or swaps. A common misunderstanding is that the forward rate trajectory represents the market’s forecast of future rates. In fact, forward rates tell you the rates you can lock in today for accrual periods starting in the future (t ≥ 0). They don’t necessarily reflect the expected market rate at time t, but rather the rate you can secure today for that future period.
The simplest forward curve calibration technique is the bootstrap method, which is used to construct a curve from the observed prices of calibration securities. For the reasons stated in the problem above, our calibration instruments will be CMTs. To begin, select a market close date from the Treasury Department’s CMT website and gather the par yields (coupon rates) for Treasury bonds with maturities from 1 to 30 years. Next, create a date grid starting from the closing date that includes the maturity dates of each bond. Then, construct a step function of instantaneous, continuously compounded discount rates, with knots based on the maturity grid. The method is called a ‘bootstrap’ because you solve sequentially for the constant rate from time 0 to 1 year that produces a price equal to par for the one-year bond, lock that rate in, and repeat the process for subsequent bonds, building on the previously determined rates, until you reach the 30-year bond.
Just a note: Your ZCB (Zero-Coupon Bond) calculator might have assumed a uniform grid of discount rates, but that’s not the case here. You may need to generalize your code further to account for the specific structure of the discount rates we’re dealing with.

title: Part IV: Forward Curves
section: Problem 16: Forward Curve - An Improved Calibration Method
text:
Problem 16: Forward Curve - An Improved Calibration Method
The discount rate grid from our bootstrapper is very coarse which can lead to big jumps in rates. Develop an alternative calibrator that uses a step function with a finer grid, such as monthly or weekly intervals, to produce the same spot bond prices while penalizing large rate jumps. This new calibrator should minimize rate jumps by incorporating a penalty function, ensuring smoother transitions between rates. You have a lot of options here, so get crazy if you want. One solution can be found in the rates I gave above.
Try applying this new curve with the coupon rate calculation function you developed in problem 15, which calculates the coupon required to produce a par price. The output for the spot calibration instruments (i.e., the calculated coupon rates or prices) should remain unchanged, but the forward rates may differ significantly. Plot both the original and new forward curves to visualize the differences.
In practice, the ‘knots’ — specific points where discount rates change — at the front end of the curve are often based on market events, such as Federal Reserve meeting dates, where interest rates may be expected to change. This approach accounts for the higher frequency and impact of market events in the near term. On the other hand, the back end of the curve typically follows a more regular approach, similar to the one used in this problem. Here, the trade-offs between using larger intervals and maintaining smoother curves are influenced by the nature of the financial products being traded.
NB: This will take a lot longer to run than your bootstrap.
